title: What do you like?
goal: Say what you like and dislike, and set up the fourth case: the dative — the case of the receiver, which Slovak uses in places you wouldn't expect, including to say that something tastes good.
bekal: tell *mať rád* and *páčiť sa* apart — two ways of saying "like" that can't be swapped
use the dative pronouns *mi, ti, mu, jej, nám, vám, im*
talk about your hobbies and free time

notes: **Two ways to say "like", and they can't be swapped.** *Mám rád* means lasting liking — a settled preference. *Páči sa mi* means liking that comes from an impression — something appeals to you. The film *páčil sa mi* (I enjoyed it last night), but old films in general *mám rád* (I'm a real fan).

**Rád follows the speaker's gender, not the thing liked.** Budi says *mám rád*, Eva says *mám rada*. This is one of the few places in A1 where you have to know your own gender to choose a word — along with *chcel/chcela by som* and the past tense in unit 13.

**Rád + verb = to like doing.** *Rád varím* = I like cooking. Not "I cook gladly" — even though that's the literal meaning. This is the most natural way to talk about hobbies that are activities, and far more common than any alternative.

**Páči sa mi uses reversed order.** The subject of the sentence is **the thing liked**, and the person goes into the dative. *Košice sa mi páčia* literally means "Košice pleases me" — and since Košice is plural, the verb is plural too. Exactly like Spanish *gustar*.
**Chutí mi works the same way.** *Halušky mi chutia* = "halušky taste good to me". Again the food is the subject. If you can use *páči sa mi*, you can use *chutí mi* straight away — it's one pattern.

grammars.title: The dative — the case of the receiver
body: The dative answers *komu?* (to whom) and *čomu?* (to what). Its main job: marking the person who receives something, or who experiences something.
after: **Notice that the feminine dative is exactly the same as the feminine locative**: *žene, škole, ulici*. One form, two jobs — a small gift that means nothing new to learn for half the nouns.

**The adjective**: m and n take **-ému** (*môjmu dobrému bratovi*), f takes **-ej** (*mojej sestre*). The feminine *-ej* now appears in three cases at once — genitive, dative, locative. Learn it once, use it three times.

**Verbs that take the dative** are the ones with a receiver: *dať* (to give), *povedať* (to say), *pomôcť* (to help), *ďakovať* (to thank), *volať* (to call), *veriť* (to believe), *rozumieť* (to understand). And the two "feeling" verbs at the heart of this unit: *páčiť sa* and *chutiť*. (Careful: *boleť* — to hurt — takes the accusative, not the dative; it's covered in unit 12.)
**Prepositions with the dative: *k* and *ku*.** *Idem k lekárovi* (I'm going to the doctor's), *ku škole* (toward the school). Unlike *do*: *k* means heading toward, *do* means going inside.

grammars.title: Dative pronouns
body: Like the accusative, dative pronouns have a short and a long form. The short form is used constantly and is never stressed.

head: Person
Short
Long
Example
rows: *Páči sa mi to.* — I like it.
*Chutí ti to?* — Do you like the taste?
*Dám mu knihu.* — I'll give him a book.

after: **The short form sits in second place** in the sentence, just like *som* and *sa*: *Ten film sa mi páčil*, *Veľmi mi chutí*. If you want to put it first for emphasis, you must use the long form: *Mne sa to páči*.

**The order is fixed when there are several short words**: *som/si* first, then *sa/si*, then the dative, then the accusative. *Páčil **sa mi** ten film.* *Dal **som mu ju**.* This order never changes, and after a few weeks your ear will reject any other.
**Mi and si are easy to mix up.** *Mi* = to me (dative). *Si* = you are (byť) **or** for oneself (*dám si*). The situation keeps them apart, and in practice it rarely confuses.

sections.title: Mať rád or páčiť sa — choosing correctly

blocks.text: **The last row matters for your social life.** *Mám ťa rád* means "I'm fond of you / I love you" — said to family, close friends, and partners. *Páčiš sa mi* means "I find you attractive" — a confession of a crush. Swapping them can send a conversation in a very different direction.

blocks.title: One form trap
items: *Páči sa mi* for one thing, *páčia sa mi* for several. The verb follows the thing, not you: *Páči sa mi tá kniha*, but *Páčia sa mi tie knihy*.
The past tense follows the thing too: *Páčil sa mi film* (m), *Páčila sa mi kniha* (f), *Páčilo sa mi mesto* (n), *Páčili sa mi Košice* (pl).

blocks.text: For sports, Slovak uses *hrať* (to play) for ball games and *chodiť na* for other activities: *hrám futbal*, *hrám hokej*, but *chodím plávať* (I go swimming), *chodím na turistiku*. Musical instruments also take *hrať na*: *hrám na gitare*.

blocks.title: Two things that bind Slovaks together
items: **Ice hockey** is the national sport, and a match against the Czechs brings the country to a standstill. If you want one conversation opener that never fails, this is it.

**Turistika** — hiking in the mountains — is an almost universal weekend activity. Slovakia has a network of color-marked trails more than 13,000 kilometers long, and almost everyone has childhood memories of the Tatras. Asking *Chodíš na turistiku?* will almost always open up a long story.
